title: Averages and charts
ks3: Statistics: mean, median, mode and range, bar charts, pie charts and scatter graphs
intro: Make sense of data. Practise the mean, median, mode and range, reading bar charts and pie charts, and spotting correlation.
description: Free KS3 Maths statistics questions with answers: mean, median, mode and range, choosing an average, bar charts, pie charts and scatter graphs. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: Find the mean of 4, 6 and 8.
questions.hint: Add them up, then divide by how many numbers there are.

questions.q: Find the mode of 3, 7, 7, 2, 9.
questions.hint: The mode is the most common value.
questions.explain: 7 appears twice and the others only once, so the mode is 7.

questions.q: Find the median of 5, 1, 9, 3, 7.
questions.hint: Put the numbers in order first, then find the middle one.
questions.explain: In order: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle number is 5.

questions.q: Find the mean of 2, 5, 9 and 4.
questions.hint: There are 4 numbers.

questions.q: Find the median of 8, 2, 6, 4.
questions.hint: In order: 2, 4, 6, 8. There are two middle numbers.
questions.explain: The two middle numbers are 4 and 6. The median is halfway between them: 5.

questions.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 8. What do the 5 numbers add up to?
questions.hint: Mean = total ÷ how many. Work backwards.
questions.explain: Total = mean × how many = 8 × 5 = 40.

questions.q: The mean of four numbers is 7. Three of them are 4, 5 and 9. What is the fourth number?
questions.hint: Find the total of all four numbers first.
questions.explain: The total must be 7 × 4 = 28. 4 + 5 + 9 = 18, so the fourth number is 28 − 18 = 10.

questions.q: Four friends have £3, £5, £6 and £10 of pocket money. What is the mean amount, in pounds?
questions.hint: Add up the amounts, then divide by how many friends there are.

questions.q: A team scored 3, 1, 5, 0, 4 and 1 goals in six matches. What is the median number of goals?
questions.hint: Put the numbers in order. With six numbers, there are two in the middle.
questions.explain: In order: 0, 1, 1, 3, 4, 5. The two middle numbers are 1 and 3, and halfway between them is 2.

questions.q: Sam's mean score in 4 spelling tests is 6. After a fifth test, the mean of all 5 tests is 7. What did Sam score in the fifth test?
questions.hint: Find the total of the first 4 tests, then the total of all 5.
questions.explain: The first 4 tests add up to 4 × 6 = 24. All 5 add up to 5 × 7 = 35. So the fifth score is 35 − 24 = 11.

questions.q: Find the range of 12, 4, 9, 20, 15.
questions.hint: Range = biggest − smallest.
questions.explain: The biggest is 20 and the smallest is 4, so the range is 20 − 4 = 16.

questions.q: A shoe shop wants to know the most popular shoe size. Which average should it use?
questions.hint: "Most popular" means the one that comes up most often.
questions.explain: The mode is the most common value. (A mean shoe size like 6.37 would not even be a real size!)

questions.q: Five people earn £20,000, £21,000, £22,000, £23,000 and £200,000 a year. Which average best shows a typical salary?
questions.hint: One salary is much bigger than the others. Which average does it pull up?
questions.explain: The median is £22,000, which is typical. The £200,000 pulls the mean up to £57,200, which is more than four of the five people earn.

questions.q: The midday temperatures for a week were 14, 17, 12, 19, 16, 15 and 13 °C. What is the range?
questions.hint: Range = highest − lowest.
questions.explain: The highest is 19 °C and the lowest is 12 °C, so the range is 19 − 12 = 7 °C.

questions.q: A set of numbers has a range of 9. The smallest number is 4. What is the largest number?
questions.hint: Range = largest − smallest. Work backwards.
questions.explain: Largest = smallest + range = 4 + 9 = 13.

questions.q: Two players each throw 5 darts. Both have a mean score of 15. Asha's scores have a range of 4 and Ben's have a range of 20. Who is more consistent?
options: Asha, because her range is smaller
Ben, because his range is bigger
They are the same, because the means are equal
You cannot tell without the median
questions.hint: A small range means the scores are close together.
questions.explain: Asha's scores are closer together (range 4), so she is more consistent. The means are the same, so the range shows the difference.

questions.q: The bar chart shows how many books a class borrowed each day. How many were borrowed on Tuesday?
questions.hint: Read across from the top of the Tuesday bar.
questions.explain: The Tuesday bar reaches 7.

questions.q: Use the bar chart. How many books were borrowed altogether from Monday to Friday?
questions.hint: Read all five bars and add them up.

questions.q: Use the bar chart. What was the mean number of books borrowed per day?
questions.hint: Mean = total ÷ number of days.
questions.explain: The total is 25 books over 5 days, so the mean is 25 ÷ 5 = 5 books per day.

questions.q: A scatter graph shows that taller students tend to have bigger feet. What kind of correlation is this?
questions.hint: As one goes up, what happens to the other?
questions.explain: When one value goes up and the other tends to go up too, it is positive correlation. The points slope upwards.

questions.q: The bar chart shows the favourite fruit of some students. Which fruit is the most popular?
questions.hint: Look for the tallest bar.
questions.explain: The Grapes bar is the tallest (8 students), so grapes are the most popular.

questions.q: Use the bar chart. How many more students chose grapes than banana?
questions.hint: Read the Grapes bar and the Banana bar, then find the difference.
questions.explain: Grapes 8 and banana 4, so 8 − 4 = 4 more students.

questions.q: A café finds that on hotter days it sells fewer hot chocolates. What kind of correlation is this?
questions.hint: As the temperature goes up, what happens to the number of hot chocolates sold?
questions.explain: When one value goes up and the other tends to go down, it is negative correlation. The points on a scatter graph slope downwards.

questions.q: 36 people are shown on a pie chart. How many degrees of the circle stand for 1 person?
questions.hint: A full circle is 360°.
questions.explain: 360° ÷ 36 = 10° for each person.

questions.q: 40 people were asked about their favourite pet. On a pie chart the "cat" slice is 90°. How many people chose cat?
questions.hint: What fraction of the whole circle is 90°?
questions.explain: 90° is {1/4} of 360°, so {1/4} of 40 = 10 people chose cat.

questions.q: On a pie chart, exactly half of the circle is for "football". What is the angle of the football slice?
questions.hint: A full circle is 360°.
questions.explain: Half of 360° is 180°.

questions.q: 60 people were asked how they like to keep fit, and 15 said swimming. What angle should the swimming slice be on a pie chart?
questions.hint: What fraction of the 60 people chose swimming?

questions.q: 120 students were asked how they get to school. On a pie chart, the "walk" slice is 135°. How many students walk?
questions.hint: Work out how many degrees stand for 1 student first.
questions.explain: 360° ÷ 120 = 3° per student, so 135° ÷ 3° = 45 students.
